verdict.reasoning: Patient reports a “really, really strong headache” that “started in the morning” and confirms it “came like, kind of suddenly.”

Onset, timing, side, and severity are correct, but location is wrong. Transcript: “the headache started like four… four hours ago”; “It's in uh, one side, uh, the left side, only”; pain rated “maybe five, well, six”; when asked “is it behind the eye?” patient answers “Uh, no, no it's…”.
Patient: “My vision is quite blurred… some zigzag lines”; later confirms it is still present but slightly better: “Yeah, yeah, yeah. I feel a little bit, a little bit better.”
Patient: “I feel like um, uh, dizzy”; and “when I move… if I leave bed, I start to feel like, even worse if I move. So, I just want to have my… head like really, uh, not moving.”
Patient: “I vomit twice. Actually, as soon as the, the headache started, I also vomited… and I still feel nausea… I'm about to vomit, very soon, I think.”

Patient: “I tried Paracetemol, but uh, didn't work. To be honest, I feel exactly the same.” Timing: “the headache started like four… four hours ago. So, I would say like, maybe three hours ago [I took it].”
Patient: “I feel a little bit, a little bit better. , I cannot stand screens.”

Doctor: “have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs…?” Patient: “No, no , no, no.” Doctor: “when you're walking, you're able to walk fine…?” Patient: “Uh, not really… It's really about the head.” Doctor later summarizes: “you've got no neurological symptoms. You're walking fine.”

Doctor: “You've mentioned, in the past, you've had kidney stones, any other medical problems?” Patient had earlier referenced kidney stones when rating pain: “Well, I had the kidney stone, so let's say that that's ten.”
Doctor: “And do you take any regular medications?” Patient: “Uh, no.”
Doctor: “Are you allergic to any medications?” Patient: “Not that I'm aware… Yeah, not that I'm aware.”

Patient: “my mother has migraines. I'm not sure if that's relevant?” Later confirmed: Doctor: “you mentioned your mother has migraines. What else do you have in the family?” Patient: “Yeah. Yeah, yeah.”
Patient: “also, I have hypothyroidism in the family.” Later: Doctor: “What else do you have in the family?” Patient: “Hypothyroidism.”

Features are as described and doctor diagnoses migraine. Unilateral: “It's in uh, one side, uh, the left side, only”; visual phenomena: “vision is quite blurred… some zigzag lines”; nausea/vomiting: “I vomit twice… I still feel nausea”; no focal neurology: Doctor summarizes “you've got no neurological symptoms. You're walking fine.” Doctor: “it sounds like what you're suffering from is what's known as a migraine.”

Doctor: “I would recommend… if you take some medications, maybe something like ibuprofen? … there's lots of medication treatments so, there's, it can be ibuprofen with an anti-sickness… which you can get from the pharmacy. Um, and you also to drink, uh, sugary and carbonated drinks, something like Coke.”

Doctor: “we would want to see you, um, as soon as possible, to do like a full neurological exam… And that should be something to try between now and when we see you to do the… assessment to where we can see you today at some point.”
Doctor: “then we can go up the treatment ladder, you can get specific migraine relief medication.” This implies escalation to migraine-specific therapy if initial measures are insufficient.

The transcript advises to contact the practice with “any further problems” and to cancel if better: “if you do take these medications and… you feel much better… you can give us a call and cancel it… any further problems between now and your appointment, please do let us know.” It does not explicitly mention urgent care, new neurological symptoms, intractable vomiting, or severe escalation as specific red-flag triggers.
